newsitem.title: USA: Black activists stage protests against Texaco.
newsitem.headline: Black activists stage protests against Texaco.

text.p: Black activists in Los Angeles and New York staged protests Saturday against embattled oil giant Texaco Inc despite the company's agreement to settle a racial discrimination lawsuit brought by black employees in 1994.

Civil rights leader Rev. Jesse Jackson, who plans to spearhead a nationwide boycott of Texaco products, told about 50 protestors outside the company's Wilmington refinery near Los Angeles, "We are glad a settlement was reached. Because of that we will apply a moratorium on picketing but the boycott will continue."
In Brooklyn, New York, Rev. Al Sharpton, led about 20 protestors in an hourlong demonstration outside a Texaco retail gasoline station.
Both demonstrations were carried out peacefully.
In Los Angeles, Jackson's speech was punctuated by honks of support from passing trucks.
He said he did not know how long the boycott would last but hoped it would end soon.

Texaco Inc. said Friday it had reached a $176 million pact to settle a racial discrimination lawsuit filed against it by six black employees in 1994. The lawsuit charged the oil giant with systematically discriminating against blacks and denying them promotions.
The plaintiffs' group, representing 1,400 black employees who joined the suit, said the settlement was the biggest in a racial discrimination case by a corporation in the United States.
"Although it was settled with 1,400 employees how many more employees are going through the same thing," asked Edna Williams, a community activist at the California protest.
In his speech at the rally Jackson demanded stricter enforcement of fair hiring practices, better enforcment of environment laws and a stronger company role in community economic development.
"In some sense that settlement does not show how good Texaco is, it shows how bad Texaco has been," he said.
In Washington, Kweisi Mfume, president of the NAACP, said Texaco had made "a good first step" toward solving problems brought on by racial and religious insensitivity of Texaco executives.
He said the NAACP would continue discussions with Texaco over next two to three weeks.

"Should those negotiations fail to bring about a specific plan of action on Texaco's part we are still prepared to move ahead with a nationwide coordinated stock divestiture campaign," Mfume said in a statement.
The negotiations will cover Texaco's hiring goals, promotional opportunties and procurement practices.
